newsitem.title: USA: Ruling on Ill. tollway expansion to be appealed.
newsitem.headline: Ruling on Ill. tollway expansion to be appealed.

text.p: A U.S. District Court ruling last month that stalled expansion of the tollway system in northeastern Illinois will be appealed, Illinois transportation officials said late Thursday.

Illinois State Toll Highway Authority and Illinois Department of Transportation said that after carefully reviewing Judge Suzanne Conlon's ruling, they believe "it is appropriate to move forward" with a planned 12.5-mile extension of I-355.
Dave Loveday, a spokesman for the tollway authority, said the appeal would be filed with the U.S. Court of Appeals by Feb 17.
"We think we have a strong case. We think we're going to win," he said.

Conlon ruled last month that Illinois failed to evaluate alternatives to the toll road or the effect the tollway extension would have on air quality. She directed state transportation officials to produce studies justifying their conclusions for the extension or explain why the studies were not possible.
The lawsuit was brought last year by the Chicago-based Environmental Law & Policy Center and other environmental groups that claimed the environmental impact statement for the project was flawed.
Conlon's ruling delayed plans by the tollway authority to issue up to $700 million of revenue bonds this spring for the toll road extension. Bear, Stearns & Co. has been tapped to lead the deal.
In their statement, the state transportation agencies said the lawsuit "is not about environmental concerns" but over the plaintiffs' "belief that new roads are bad and must be stopped."

"Inflicting costly delays as a way to kill the road is the real goal of the plaintiffs," the statement said, adding that studies already document the need for extending I-355 into the growing Will County region.

Howard Learner, executive director of the environmental center, said the public officials "time, energy and taxpayers money would be better spent on complying with the U.S. District Court's order and developing better transportation alternatives for the people of the Chicago area."
